newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel says to ready Germany for EMU on time.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel says to ready Germany for EMU on time.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday pledged that Germany would do everything possible to fulfil entry criteria for currency union and said any talk now of delaying the 1999 start date would be wrong.

"Germany will do everything to meet the criteria" for Europe's planned economic union, Waigel told a meeting of city governments, echoing Chancellor Helmut Kohl's determination to keep the project on track in spite of recent setbacks.

As Germany, once the role model for European economic integration, itself struggles to meet the strict fiscal entry criteria for the euro currency, some politicians have argued that a delay would be a wise, giving all nations more time to meet goals.
Ringed by journalists, Waigel brushed off talk of pushing out the launch date, saying: "Currently we are in the middle of the year that will decide currency union. So talk of a delay would be wrong."
Next spring EU nations will present their 1997 economic statistics to European government leaders who will decide which countries will qualify to join the union in the first wave.
Waigel, however, gave few details of how he planned to plug the nation's gaping budget deficit in time to secure German membership in EMU, long considered Kohl's dearest wish.
Repeating largely what he told parliamentarians on Wednesday, he said: "All future expenditures over one million marks will have to be approved by me."

He also said that privatisation "will be continued or may even be stepped up", hinting again that Bonn might try to find new funds by privatising postal bank Postbank, highway rest-stops and more of its stake in telecommunications group Deutsche Telekom.
But Waigel promised that the government would not sell off parts of Germany's gold reserves, as other European nations have done, to prepare for currency union.

"The sale of gold is out of the question," he said, trying to calm frayed public nerves about Bonn's controversial plans to revalue assets and use some of the paper profits to meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria.
His credibility badly bruised after an unusually public row with the Bundesbank, Waigel also tried to set the record straight on his controversial plan.
"Not one mark of any paid-out profits from any revaluation would flow into the budget. All the money would go to scale back debt acquired through unification," he said.

Bonn last month unveiled plans to value currency and gold assets closer to market levels and receive a "payout" of these unrealised profits this year, a move which the Bundesbank compared to accounting tricks used elsewhere in Europe.

Waigel and Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, however, appeared to have moved closer to finding a compromise to the issue earlier this week with both stressing that relations between the two sides were constructive.

Pressed several times to comment on details of a possible compromise, Waigel said only that talks with the central bank were constructive and that he could only repeat comments made by Tietmeyer a day erlier.
"We are having talks with the Bundesbank and only after that can a decision be reached on a change to the Bundesbank law," Waigel said.
Waigel welcomed the release of first-quarter gross domestic product data showing 0.5 percent quarter-on-quarter growth and 1.4 percent year-on-year growth.
"The new indicators are positive," he said, adding: "They could have a positive impact on the deficit."
But he said the numbers were unlikely to have a major impact on Germany's stubbornly high unemployment rate.

Fresh from surviving a motion in parliament to sack him on Wednesday, Waigel faced hordes of camera teams in a more relaxed mood, stopping several times on the way to his car and joking that he was surprised there had not been more such uncomfortable moments during his eight-year tenure.
